turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Contemptuously, you say? I daresay Mr. Wickham’s misfortunes are quite fashionable to lament, aren’t they, Mr. Darcy? It is remarkably convenient to cast one’s own failings onto the misfortunes of another, is it not?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Indeed, Miss Bennet, I find your levity on this matter most perplexing. To suggest I derive some personal gratification from Mr. Wickham’s…difficulties…is an assertion born of a profound misunderstanding of my character and a deliberate disregard for the truth.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A profound misunderstanding, you say? Perhaps it is *I* who misunderstand *you*, Mr. Darcy. Your indignation seems disproportionate to the simple observation that you display a peculiar interest in the misfortunes of those you clearly disapprove of.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your persistent attempts to misinterpret my actions and motives are quite tiresome. I find myself compelled to state, despite the obvious discomfort this may cause you, that my regard for you extends far beyond mere acquaintance; I am, in truth, deeply and irrevocably in love with you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Love? Mr. Darcy, you insult my ears as much as you attempt my understanding. I find it difficult to credit such a declaration from a gentleman who has, until this moment, made every effort to render me disagreeable.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I perceive your incredulity, and I confess, the manner in which I have previously conducted myself has done little to encourage such sentiments. However, to suggest that my actions have been solely intended to render you disagreeable is a gross misrepresentation of my struggles against my own reason and, indeed, my own heart.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Struggles, Mr. Darcy? You speak of struggles as if battling a fearsome dragon, when in truth, your struggle appears to have been a determined effort to prove yourself superior to everyone within a ten-mile radius! Pray, enlighten me: what precisely was so objectionable about me that required such elaborate, and frankly, offensive attempts at distancing?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your assessment is, as usual, coloured by a regrettable tendency towards hyperbole. The truth is far more complex than your flippant observations allow; I have been hampered by considerations of propriety, by the disparity in our stations, and, I confess, by a painful awareness of the impropriety my affections would engender within my circle. It is not a matter of proving myself superior, but of upholding a standard, a duty which, it appears, you find difficult to comprehend.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A standard, Mr. Darcy? A duty? Is that what you call it, this calculated disdain? I daresay your 'standard' is merely a convenient excuse for your own pride, a justification for treating those beneath you with a condescension that would shame a tradesman.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, you mistake my intentions entirely! My concern has never been to inflict offense, but to navigate a situation fraught with potential ruin – ruin not merely for myself, but for your family as well. To accuse me of condescension is to fundamentally misunderstand the delicate balance required when one is tasked with upholding the honour of a lineage and protecting the vulnerable from societal disgrace.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Protecting my family, you say? How very noble of you, Mr. Darcy. It seems your 'duty' extends only to the preservation of your own reputation, conveniently disguised as concern for others.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your persistent misinterpretations are… vexing. I assure you, my actions have been motivated by a sincere desire to shield those I hold dear, even from themselves, and to preserve a sense of decorum that, regrettably, appears lost upon you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Shield them from themselves? Really, Mr. Darcy? It appears your definition of 'protection' involves dictating their lives and condemning them for daring to aspire to happiness outside your approved sphere. I find your self-righteousness quite astonishing.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I confess, I find your accusations increasingly difficult to endure. To suggest that my concern for propriety stems solely from a desire to preserve my own reputation is a gross distortion of my character and a profound lack of understanding regarding the responsibilities inherent in my station.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Responsibilities? Is that what you call it, Mr. Darcy? It seems to me a rather convenient justification for meddling, a shield behind which you hide your own pride and prejudice. I daresay a man of true honour would not feel the need to 'protect' others by controlling their choices.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I find your continued insistence on portraying me as a meddling tyrant… deeply unfair. My intentions, however imperfectly perceived, have always been rooted in a desire for the betterment of those around me, though I concede my methods may have, at times, been… misguided.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Misguided, you say? A most agreeable admission, Mr. Darcy, though it scarcely begins to atone for the liberties you have taken. Do you truly believe that a clumsy apology and a vague acknowledgement of error will erase the damage you have inflicted upon my family’s happiness?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your words wound me more deeply than you may comprehend. I have endeavoured to explain my actions, to illuminate the motivations behind them, yet you persist in viewing me through a lens of malice and misunderstanding; I confess, I am at a loss to understand how to bridge this chasm between us.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Illuminating motivations? Mr. Darcy, you speak of understanding, yet you seem utterly incapable of perceiving the pain you have caused. I find it exceedingly difficult to credit your supposed desire for betterment when your actions consistently demonstrate a profound disregard for the feelings of others.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I perceive a certain… enjoyment, even, in your condemnation of me. Perhaps you find satisfaction in portraying me as the villain of your own narrative? I assure you, my conduct, though undoubtedly flawed, stems not from a desire to inflict pain, but from a deeply ingrained sense of what I believe to be right and proper.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: She answered him with cold civility.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His sense of her inferiority, of its being a degradation, of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: He concluded with representing to her the strength of that attachment which in spite of all his endeavours he had found impossible to conquer; and with expressing his hope that it would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! repeated Darcy, contemptuously--yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
